title: Making and moving files
objectives: Create, copy, move and delete files and folders from the terminal.
Use a `*` wildcard to act on many files at once.
Check where you are before deleting, because `rm` has no undo.

screens.prose:
You downloaded two price files and want them in your data folder. In your home folder you type two commands:

```sh
$ mv Downloads/prices.csv data/
$ cp Downloads/trades.csv data/
```
screens.question: Drag each file to the folder it is in after both commands.

hints.text: mv is short for move and cp for copy. What does each leave behind?
Both files start in Downloads.
Moving takes prices.csv out of Downloads. Copying leaves trades.csv there and puts a second one in data.

feedback.correct: prices.csv moved; trades.csv now exists in both folders.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A move leaves nothing behind; a copy leaves the original.

byKey.p: You left prices.csv in Downloads, or put it in both. mv moves the file: nothing stays behind.
byKey.t1: One trades.csv belongs in each folder. cp makes a copy and leaves the original where it was.
byKey.t2: One trades.csv belongs in each folder. cp makes a copy and leaves the original where it was.

explain.text: mv took prices.csv out of Downloads and put it in data. cp left trades.csv in Downloads and put a copy in data. Both name the file first, then where it should go.

screens.prose:
Downloads has filled up. Moving files one at a time is slow, so you try a pattern with a star in it:

```sh
$ cd ~/Downloads
$ ls *.csv
```
screens.question: Tap every file you expect this `ls` to list.

hints.text: What do the names you pick have to end with?
This one contains csv but ends in something else.
Pick every name that ends in .csv, whatever comes before it.

feedback.correct: Three names end in .csv, so three are listed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every name that ends in .csv, and only those.

byKey.contains: You included trades.csv.bak. It contains csv, but the pattern needs the name to end in .csv.
byKey.exact: You left out prices_2024.csv. The star matches any run of characters, including prices_2024.

explain.text: The star matched prices, trades and prices_2024, so three files were listed. trades.csv.bak was left out because it ends in .bak. The pattern must match the whole name, start to end.

screens.prose:
The star is a **wildcard**: it stands for any characters, even none. The shell swaps the pattern for every matching name before the command runs. So wildcards work with `mv` and `cp` too. Still in Downloads, you type:

```sh
$ mv *.csv ~/data/
```
screens.question: Drag each file to the folder it is in afterwards.

hints.text: Which names does `*.csv` match? You found them on the last screen.
These three end in .csv.
The three .csv files move to data. The rest stay in Downloads.

feedback.correct: The three .csv files moved; the rest stayed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move exactly the names that end in .csv.

byKey.f5: trades.csv.bak ends in .bak, so the pattern does not match it. It stays in Downloads.
byKey.f2: prices_2024.csv ends in .csv, so the star matches it. It moves with the others.
byKey.f3: notes.txt does not end in .csv, so it stays in Downloads.
byKey.f4: chart.png does not end in .csv, so it stays in Downloads.

explain.text: The shell turned `*.csv` into three names, then mv moved all three. One command did the work of three. The other files never matched, so they stayed put.

canvas.caption: The shaded files moved to data

screens.prose:
`mv` has a second job. Give it a new name instead of a folder, and it renames the file:

```sh
$ cd ~/data
$ mv prices.csv prices_old.csv
$ ls
```
screens.question: What does `ls` print?

options.why: You treated mv like cp. A move, or a rename, leaves nothing behind.

options.text: A new folder, prices_old.csv, holding prices.csv
options.why: mv moves into a folder only when that folder already exists. Here it does not, so mv renames.

options.text: An error, because prices_old.csv does not exist
options.why: The second name does not need to exist. mv gives the file that name.

hints.text: Does a folder called prices_old.csv exist?
This is the file being renamed.
No such folder exists, so mv gives prices.csv the new name. Nothing else changes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no folder of that name, mv renames.

explain.text: A rename is a move to a new name in the same folder. The contents of the file did not change. If prices_old.csv had already existed, mv would have replaced it without asking.

screens.prose:
`mkdir` makes a new, empty folder: `mkdir results` creates results. You are home, where data already holds your price files, and type:

```sh
$ mkdir data
```
screens.question: What happens?

options.text: mkdir refuses, and data is untouched
data is replaced by a new, empty folder
options.why: You expected mkdir to overwrite. It never touches a folder that already exists.

options.text: A second folder called data appears
options.why: One folder cannot hold two items with the same name.
The shell never picks a new name for you. It does exactly what you typed, or stops.

hints.text: Can one folder hold two items with the same name?
data is already here.
The name is taken, so mkdir stops with an error and changes nothing.

feedback.correct: mkdir stops: the name is taken.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what happens when the name is already in use.

explain.text: On a Mac, mkdir replies `mkdir: data: File exists`, and nothing inside data changes. Linux words the error differently. mkdir is safe to get wrong; the next command is not.

screens.prose:
`rm` removes. You are home and type two commands:

```sh
$ rm notes.txt
$ rm data
```
screens.question: What happens to the folder data?

options.text: rm refuses, because data is a folder, so it stays
data and the files in it are deleted
options.why: Plain rm deletes files only. Deleting a folder needs an extra letter, which comes next.

options.text: Only the files inside data are deleted
options.why: rm does not reach inside folders unless you ask it to. Here it stops at the folder.
rm never uses the Bin. What it deletes is gone.

hints.text: Is data a file or a folder?
data is a folder.
Plain rm works on files. Given a folder, it prints an error and leaves it alone.

feedback.correct: Plain rm deletes files, not folders.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what plain rm does with a folder.

explain.text: rm refuses with `rm: data: is a directory` on a Mac, or `Is a directory` on Linux, so data survives. notes.txt, though, is gone for good, with no Bin. To delete a folder and all it holds you add `-r`, for recursive.

screens.prose:
You are tidying up. An old copy of your data sits in ~/projects/data, and you mean to delete it. You type:

```sh
$ pwd
/Users/ana
$ rm -r data
```

params.aria: Folder tree of the home folder

state.caption: The blue ring is where you are.

screens.question: Tap everything that is now deleted.

hints.text: Where does a bare name like data point: from where you are, or from where you meant?
You are in ana, and this is the data folder directly inside it.
rm -r removed ~/data and everything inside it. The old copy in projects is untouched.

feedback.correct: rm -r deleted ~/data and both files inside it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the path data from where you are, ana.

byKey.intended: You tapped the copy you meant to delete. rm reads data from where you are, ana, so it removed ~/data instead.
byKey.intended-folder: You tapped the copy you meant to delete. rm reads data from where you are, ana, so it removed ~/data instead.
byKey.folder-only: The -r means recursive: rm also removed everything inside data, both price files.
byKey.pdata: That is the copy you meant to delete. rm reads data from where you are, ana, so it removed ~/data instead.

explain.text: `rm -r data` removed ~/data with both price files, and the old copy survived. There is no Bin and no undo in the terminal. Before any rm -r, run pwd and ls to check what the name points at.

screens.prose:
Each command names what to act on first, then where it goes:

```sh
$ mkdir results
$ cp a.csv results/
$ mv a.csv b.csv
$ rm b.csv
$ rm -r results
$ ls *.csv
```

In order: a new empty folder, a copy that keeps the original, a rename or move, a delete with no undo, a folder and all inside it, and the names ending .csv.
screens.question: Before you press Enter on an `rm -r`, what should you run?

options.text: `pwd`, then `ls` on the folder you mean to delete
Nothing: the Bin keeps a copy
options.why: The terminal has no Bin. A deleted file is gone.

options.text: Plain `rm` on the folder first, as a test
options.why: Plain rm refuses every folder, so it tells you nothing about which folder you named.
mkdir makes an empty folder. It copies nothing into it.

hints.text: What went wrong on the last screen?
The name data pointed somewhere you did not expect.
pwd tells you where you are; ls shows what the name you typed points at.

feedback.correct: Check where you are and what the name points at.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about the mistake on the last screen.

explain.text: The rm -r went wrong because data meant a different folder from where you stood. pwd shows where you are. ls on the target shows exactly what is about to disappear.

screens.prose: You downloaded a year of daily prices, prices_2024.csv, into ~/Downloads. Your backtest lives in ~/projects/backtest and needs its own copy, in a new data folder inside it. Your original download must stay where it is.
screens.question: Put the commands in order.

hints.text: Where must you be before you make the new data folder?
Move into backtest, make data there, copy the file in, then list data to check.

feedback.correct: Go there, make the folder, copy, then check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each command relies on the one before it.

byKey.mk: You made data before moving into backtest. In your home folder, data already exists, so mkdir would refuse.
byKey.cp: You copied before the data folder existed. cp would have nowhere to put the file and would stop with an error.
byKey.ls: You checked before the copy. ls data would show an empty folder, or an error.

explain.text: cd puts you in backtest, so the relative name data means the new folder there. cp, not mv, leaves your original download in place. The final ls is the habit that catches mistakes before they cost you.

ideas: `mkdir` makes a folder, `cp` copies, `mv` moves or renames, and `rm` deletes.
A wildcard like `*.csv` stands for every name that ends in .csv.
`rm` and `rm -r` have no Bin and no undo, so check `pwd` and `ls` first.

formula.name: Copy and move
formula.note: What to act on comes first; where it goes comes second.

summary.trap: A bare name like data points from where you are. `rm -r data` in the wrong folder deletes the wrong data, for good.

quiz.prose:
A folder holds three files: prices.csv, trades.csv and notes.txt. You run this inside it:

```sh
$ rm *.csv
```
quiz.question: How many files are left?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the names that end in .csv.

byKey.none: You let the star match everything. `*.csv` only matches names ending in .csv.
byKey.all: You expected rm to ask first. It deletes without asking.
byKey.one-gone: The pattern matched two names, not one. rm deleted both.

explain.text: The shell expanded the pattern to prices.csv and trades.csv, and rm deleted both. notes.txt does not end in .csv, so it stayed.

quiz.prose:
A folder holds only prices.csv. You run:

```sh
$ cp prices.csv backup.csv
$ ls
```
quiz.question: What does `ls` print?

options.why: You treated cp like mv. A copy leaves the original in place.
cp made a new file, backup.csv, beside the original.

feedback.correct: Two files with the same contents.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A copy leaves the original.

explain.text: cp made a second file, backup.csv, with the same contents. prices.csv is still there. ls lists both, in alphabetical order.

quiz.prose:
You are in /Users/ana/projects, which holds report.csv. You run:

```sh
$ mv report.csv ..
```
quiz.question: Where is report.csv now?

options.why: `..` is a folder that always exists, the parent. So mv moves the file into it.
mv always moves or renames. Here it moved the file up one level.

feedback.correct: `..` is the parent folder, so the file moved up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what `..` names.

explain.text: `..` names the parent folder, /Users/ana. Because that folder exists, mv moved report.csv into it.

quiz.prose: A folder called old holds last year's backtest results. You no longer need any of it.
quiz.question: Which command deletes old and everything in it?

options.why: Plain rm refuses folders. It replies that old is a directory.
mv needs a second name, where to put it. It never deletes.

feedback.correct: `-r` lets rm go into the folder.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Plain rm only deletes files.

explain.text: `-r` makes rm recursive: it deletes old and everything inside it. Check with pwd and ls first, because there is no undo.
